cover.alt: Bjarni and Siggi buy grain at the trading post after selling their three ewes.
cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour, established visual bible, Vopnafjörður in June 1875. Timber store by the fjord, black Danish merchant ship at anchor in the background. Fully clothed Hansen in a waistcoat beside the scales, Bjarni counting his few coins, Siggi beside him. Exactly two packhorses with packs; exactly three grain sacks at the trading post; three thin ewes with Bjarni’s straight-tip-cut earmarks left with Hansen, separate from the horses. A small bag of sugar for afi and Ásta is with Siggi, still unopened. No coffee purchase, free relief-grain distribution, modern objects or lettering.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Afi segir: „Við sjóinn. Þar kaupir fólk korn og kaffi.“
Í kaupstaðnum kaupir fólk og selur.
Bjarni seldi kindur og keypti korn. Hansen skrifaði í bókina.
Siggi keypti sykur fyrir afa og Ástu. Peningur afa var ekki fyrir skuldina.
words_with_history.note_en: Kaupstaður combines kaup, “buying/trade”, with staður, “place”. The history brief names the Danish firm Ørum & Wulff at Vopnafjörður. [?] Hansen, this debt book and the specific June transaction are fictional; the firm’s exact shipping arrangements here remain unverified.

pronunciation_note.rule: In þagði and sagði, ð is the voiced th of English this, not the voiceless th of thin. In keypti and þekkti the dental ending is t; in taldi and seldi it is d. Say the whole word rather than inserting a vowel between the stem and the ending.

grammar.note_en:
A weak past marks past time with a dental consonant: ð, d or t. The older -aði class is still active: kallaði (s035) means “called”; hugsaði (s027), “thought”; borgaði (s071), “paid”; skrifaði (s081), “wrote”. This chapter adds the other weak patterns. A stem is the part to which an ending attaches. The consonants beside the ending help determine its shape, but the past stem can also change its vowel, so learn the encountered word together with its ending.

For this chapter’s verbs the working groups are -ði after a vowel or r/f/g: horfa → horfði, “look → looked”; segja → sagði, “say → said”; þegja → þagði, “be silent → was silent”. The -di group follows l/n/m: telja → taldi, “count → counted”; selja → seldi, “sell → sold”; senda → sendi, “send → sent”. No m-final example is supplied in the story; it is part of the spelling explanation, not an extra table cell. The -ti group follows p/k/s/t: kaupa → keypti, “buy → bought”; þekkja → þekkti, “recognise → recognised”; flytja → flutti, “carry/transport → carried/transported”. The singular flutti is given here only to explain the spelling behind the story’s plural fluttu, not as an attested singular table cell. No s-final example occurs here. These are practical stem groups for the verbs met here, not a claim that every verb with those final consonants belongs to this class. The already known -aði class retains its own ending.

Some past stems change their vowel as well as taking a dental ending. Compare telja–taldi, selja–seldi, flytja–flutti, segja–sagði, þegja–þagði and kaupa–keypti. Umlaut is a vowel change historically caused by a vowel in a following syllable, sometimes one no longer visible. It helps explain pairs such as kaupa/keypti; it does not mean that every stem change follows one easy modern replacement rule. Do not simply add -ði to the whole infinitive or turn every -ja into the same past vowel. Spurði (s008), “asked”, likewise belongs to the weak past now available productively.

In a dictionary, a four-part citation lists the infinitive, present third-person singular, past third-person singular and supine: kaupa – kaupir – keypti – keypt, “to buy – buys – bought – [supine] bought”. The infinitive is the naming form, “to buy”; the supine is a non-finite dictionary form, without person or number. It is supplied here as reference only. This chapter does not form compound tenses, use geta with a supine, ask for supines or practise unseen first- and second-person past endings. The dictionary reference is separate from the story-based tables.

The plural uses -u after the dental consonant: horfði → horfðu (s047), “looked” with several subjects; fluttu (s127), “carried”, with hestarnir, “the horses”; sagði → sögðu (s111), “said/told”, with the ravens. The a → ö of sögðu is u-umlaut before the plural u. The third-person tables quote only cells present in the prose. There are no ég or þú past cells to fill or memorise.

The table sentences mean: Hann taldi kindurnar (s005), “He counted the ewes”; Til Vopnafjarðar, sagði Bjarni (s009), “‘To Vopnafjörður,’ said Bjarni”; Siggi horfði á kindurnar (s010), “Siggi looked at the ewes”; Hár úr halanum á Búkollu! kallaði hann (s035), “‘A hair from Búkolla’s tail!’ he called”; Bjarni þagði (s064), “Bjarni was silent”; Þá seldi Bjarni Hansen þrjár kindur (s080), “Then Bjarni sold Hansen three ewes”; Á hverjum morgni sendi hann þá út um allan heim (s110), “Every morning he sent them out throughout the whole world”; Svo keypti Bjarni þrjá poka af korni (s082), “Then Bjarni bought three sacks of grain”; Siggi þekkti þau (s138), “Siggi recognised them”. Þeir horfðu á hann og Sigga (s047) means “They looked at him and Siggi”; Hestarnir fluttu kornið (s127), “The horses carried the grain”; Þá voru þeir á öxlunum á honum og sögðu honum fréttirnar í eyrun (s111), “Then they were on his shoulders and told him the news into his ears”. Table quotations can be clauses extracted from a longer segment; the segment references identify their source.

Keep supported expressions intact: þurfti (s142) in Nú þurfti Siggi ekki hrafna, “Now Siggi did not need ravens”, is the past of þarf, “needs”; þurfa belongs to a small irregular group learnt later, so the form is shown here, not practised; af því að (s079, s115) means “because”, answering af hverju, “why”; vildi (s106, s115) means “wanted”; Eruð þér (s054), “Are you”, and Hafið þér (s089), “Have you”, address Hansen politely with plural verb forms. Þrjár kindur (s080), “three ewes”, þrjá poka (s082), “three sacks”, and tvo hrafna (s109), “two ravens”, are supported accusative numeral phrases, not numeral drills. Komdu (s038), “come” to Siggi alone, and Komið inn (s146), “come in” to the family, are supported commands. The full imperative, numeral, modal and clause systems come later. Í nótt in s101/s103 is “tonight”; dugði fyrir skuldinni (s081), “was enough to pay the debt”; voru eftir (s094), “remained behind”.
